questions.question: Explain why countries trade, using South African examples.
questions.expected_answer: Trade is the exchange of goods and services, internally or internationally. Resources are unevenly distributed: South Africa has large reserves of platinum, manganese, chromium, gold, coal and iron ore but little oil, so it imports most crude oil, while Saudi Arabia, Nigeria and Angola export oil. Climate differs, so tropical products such as tea, coffee, cocoa and bananas come from tropical regions while South Africa exports citrus, grapes, apples and wine and imports rice and coffee. Skills, technology and capital differ, so some countries make aircraft, chips and medicines. Through specialisation and comparative advantage, countries produce what they do most efficiently and trade for the rest; South Africa mines platinum and imports phones. Demand for variety gives consumers choice at lower prices. Trade earns export income, creates jobs, gives access to goods and technology and builds relationships, but can cause dependence on a few exports, competition that closes local factories and unequal relationships.

questions.question: Define imports, exports and the balance of trade, and describe South Africa's trade and trade agreements.
questions.expected_answer: Exports are goods and services sold to other countries and imports are bought from them; the balance of trade is exports minus imports, giving a surplus if exports are greater and a deficit if imports are greater. South Africa exports platinum group metals, gold, coal, iron ore, manganese and chromium, vehicles and parts from factories in the Eastern Cape, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, machinery, and agricultural products such as citrus, grapes, apples, wine, nuts and wool, as well as tourism services; it imports crude oil and fuels, machinery and electrical equipment, vehicles and parts, chemicals and medicines, and foods such as rice and wheat. China has been its largest partner, with the United States, Germany, the UK, Japan, India, the Middle East and African neighbours also important. It belongs to SACU, dating from 1910, with tariff-free trade among members, SADC and the African Continental Free Trade Area, under which trading began in 2021, and trades under WTO rules. Countries dependent on one export, such as Botswana on diamonds or Zambia on copper, try to diversify.

questions.question: Explain the links between trade and transport.
questions.expected_answer: Trade depends on transport to move goods from producers to markets, and transport cost, speed and reliability determine what can be traded and at what price. Historically, trans-Saharan caravans and Indian Ocean shipping with the monsoon carried trade, and the industrial revolution's steamships and railways expanded it, followed by trucks, aircraft and pipelines. Containerisation from the 1950s packs goods into standard twenty- or forty-foot containers moved by crane between trucks, trains and ships without unpacking, making trade faster, cheaper and safer, with port traffic measured in TEUs. About four-fifths of world trade by volume goes by sea because it is cheapest for heavy goods, while air carries little by volume but much by value. Hubs such as Durban, the busiest container port, linked to Gauteng by road, rail and pipeline, and O. R. Tambo airport connect modes, and landlocked neighbours depend on South African and Mozambican ports. Slow, costly or unreliable transport raises prices and makes exports less competitive, so infrastructure improvement increases trade.
